output.title: Second opinions should be a gate, not a guess
output.body:
If you want AI in a small business workflow, treat second opinions as a design constraint: decide up front when the system should flag a task for human review instead of acting on its own. That is not a limitation. It is the control that keeps the owner in charge.

The clearest boundary is money movement and other high-risk decisions: human approval stays mandatory. For routine work like data entry, customer replies, or document classification, you can define a review rule in the pilot, such as a confidence threshold or a simple exception list. The point is not to automate everything. The point is to make the handoff visible.

A practical question for any workflow is this: which decision would cost you more to reverse than to pause for five minutes? Write those down first. That gives you the second-opinion gate. Everything outside that boundary can stay manual or use a lighter check.

One useful next step is to map a single recurring workflow and mark each decision as “human only,” “AI can suggest,” or “AI can act.” If you are testing Bareni’s approach, keep the scope narrow, define the measures, and put the accounts in your name from the start. In the accounts-payable demo, that same approval gate is shown with synthetic data and a simulated blocked payment, not a real transfer.
